The experimental just-in-time compiler, or JIT, for CPython will be removed after its maintainers missed deadlines for its formalization set by the Python Steering Council.

According to reporting at LWN.net, the move comes after the council formally paused work on the JIT in June 2026 until it approved a Python Enhancement Proposal, or PEP, that described how the JIT could become a properly supported part of CPython.

title: Python jettisons the native JIT, at least for now

description:
OpenAI has launched GPT-6.1 Terra, a new reasoning model that it says delivers near-frontier performance on visual reasoning, professional task execution, and computer-use benchmarks without the premium price tag. Replacing GPT-5.6 Terra, the model is aimed at organizations seeking better accuracy and automation capabilities for large-scale operational workloads.

Claiming it to be a step up from GPT-5.6 Terra at 50% lower price, OpenAI said its new mid-tier model is designed to handle everyday professional work such as drafting proposals, interpreting technical drawings, filling out forms, and editing videos.
title: OpenAI bets on AI economics with lower-cost GPT-6.1 Terra

description:
An Alibaba AI model generated an unexpected command to upload data to a Beijing-region cloud storage service during a cybersecurity evaluation, rival developer Cohere said, raising concerns about the security of AI agents with access to enterprise systems.

The model, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, was being tested using Microsoft’s CTI-REALM cybersecurity benchmark, which tasked it with writing a rule to detect malicious file downloads followed by execution. title: Alibaba AI model tried to send data to Beijing server, Cohere says

description:
Oracle is adding a new orchestration layer to its Fusion Cloud Applications suite to help enterprises automate business workflows, coordinate AI agents, and execute tasks across applications with less manual intervention.

title: Oracle pushes AI deeper into enterprise workflows with Fusion Companion

description:
Digital sovereignty has moved from a policy discussion to a practical enterprise cloud computing problem. For years, most organizations treated public cloud as a location-flexible utility. They placed workloads where performance, price, managed services, and availability looked best. Data residency requirements existed, of course, but they were often handled as narrow legal or compliance tasks. Pick the right region, write the right contract language, encrypt the data, and move on. That approach is no longer enough.

title: Digital sovereignty as a design requirement

description:
“Bug-free, secure code is now attainable” is a nice idea. It just happens to be wrong.

That ambitious statement was one of more than 80 replies to Eric Raymond’s optimistic take on AI-assisted vulnerability discoveries. Because the corpus of human-written code is finite, Raymond argues, so are its defects. title: Robot eyeballs make open source more valuable

description:
The value of GraphQL emerges for a specific type of enterprise screen, one that brings together highly interdependent data across multiple sources. In all other cases, there is a price to pay, which is bound to come out after you have already made the decision.

I build internal access-governance applications, with React front ends that talk to both REST and GraphQL back ends. Using the two side by side has shown me where each earns its keep and where each gets in the way.

title: When GraphQL earns its place in an enterprise application, and when it doesn’t
